input:
The Chilton-Colburn analogy draws a direct parallel between the transfer processes by setting the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ equal to half of the friction factor $f$, a relationship that can be written compactly as

$j_D$ = $f/2$

It is worth pausing on what this statement actually involves. It is an equality between two ratios that are formed from quite different processes, with $j_D$ being obtained from a measured mass-transfer rate and $f$ being obtained from a measured pressure loss. In those situations where the two happen to be formed from one and the same surface action, the equality provides an elegant summary of the measurements on both sides. That action is skin friction: the resistance at the surface is the drag of the fluid as it moves along the surface, and it is precisely the same surface motion that is responsible both for dragging on the flow and for carrying material to and from the surface itself.

A brief numerical check helps to fix the arithmetic involved. If we take a surface for which $f$ = 0.0064, the analogy immediately gives $j_D$ = 0.0064 / 2 = 0.0032, and a measured value of $j_D$ for that surface can be compared against this figure: agreement lends support to the analogy for the surface concerned, whereas any disagreement indicates a surface where the shared action does not account for the whole of the resistance.

There is, however, an important qualification, namely the case in which pressure forces acting on the body make their own contribution to the measured resistance. Flow across a bluff body is the standard example of this: a large part of the drag is form drag, arising from pressure acting on the projected area of the body, and there is no corresponding action transferring material at the surface. The value of $f$ that is formed from the total drag consequently exceeds the skin-friction component, while $j_D$ continues to respond to the surface action alone, with the result that the measured $j_D$ falls below $f/2$. The analogy should therefore be understood as a statement about surfaces whose resistance is skin friction; where form drag is present, applying it will overstate the transfer factor by the share of the drag that is supplied by pressure forces.

The analogy then gives $j_D$ = 0.0064 / 2 = 0.0032, and a measured $j_D$ for the surface can be set against that figure directly: agreement supports the analogy for the surface in question, and the check costs nothing beyond the two measured quantities themselves, which is the attraction of the analogy as a working tool in the first place, disagreement of any size marks a surface where the shared action is not the whole of the resistance.
